```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 9,
  fig.height = 8,
  fig.align = "center",
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  dev = "png",
  dpi = 150
)
```

This vignette maps population density in India for 2011 and 2031. We use
`population_projections()` for population and the 2011 district boundaries for
area.

We make three types of map. A fill map shows density. A bubble map also shows
population size. In a dot density map, each dot shows a fixed number of people.

The national maps stop at district level. The last section shows one state at
subdistrict and village level. The totals for 2031 are IIPS projections. This
package calculates the rural and urban figures (see `?population_projections`).
Gray areas have no district data, except on the black map.

```{r load}
library(censusindia)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(sf)
```

## Density by district

We get the districts for two years, attach the boundaries, and calculate density.

```{r data}
districts <- population_projections("district", year = c(2011, 2031)) |>
  select(year, sector, state_name_harmonized, district, population) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = c(sector, year), values_from = population) |>
  attach_geometry(2011, geography = "district")

districts <- districts |>
  filter(!st_is_empty(geometry)) |>
  mutate(
    area = area_km2(geometry),
    density_2011 = total_2011 / area,
    density_2031 = total_2031 / area,
    density_change = percent_change(density_2031, density_2011),
    rural_density_2031 = pmax(rural_2031 / area, 1),
    total_millions = total_2031 / 1e6,
    urban_millions = urban_2031 / 1e6
  )
```

Density has a large range. We use one log scale for the two maps.

```{r fill-maps, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "District density maps of India, 2011 and 2031."}
compare_maps(
  list(
    "2011" = mutate(districts, density = density_2011),
    "2031" = mutate(districts, density = density_2031)
  ),
  "density",
  palette = "oranges", limits = c(1, 50000), trans = "log10", oob = scales::squish,
  breaks = c(10, 100, 1000, 10000), labels = scales::label_comma(),
  legend_title = "People per km²", na_color = "grey85",
  state_boundary_color = "white", state_boundary_width = 0.2, legend_position = "bottom"
) &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Density on a black map

A district with high density is bright, and a district with low density is dark.
The colors show calculated density. This map is not a satellite image of lights
at night. Areas with no district data are black.

```{r black-map, dev.args = list(bg = "black"), fig.alt = "District density map of India on a black background. Dense areas are bright."}
plot_map(districts, "density_2031",
  title = "Population density by district, 2031",
  palette = "inferno", dark = TRUE, trans = "log10",
  limits = c(10, 50000), oob = scales::squish,
  breaks = c(10, 100, 1000, 10000), labels = scales::label_comma(),
  legend_title = "People per km²",
  show_state_boundaries = TRUE, state_boundary_width = 0.1
)
```

The next map shows the same density with dots. Each dot shows 50,000 people. The
dot color shows the density of its district. We put each dot at a random position
in its district.

```{r black-map-dots, dev.args = list(bg = "black"), fig.alt = "Dot density map of India on a black background, one dot per 50,000 people. Dense areas are bright."}
set.seed(2031)
plot_dot_density_map(districts, "total_2031",
  per_dot = 5e4, color = "density_2031", dark = TRUE,
  trans = "log10", limits = c(10, 50000), oob = scales::squish,
  breaks = c(10, 100, 1000, 10000), labels = scales::label_comma(),
  color_title = "People per km²",
  title = "One dot for every 50,000 people, 2031",
  subtitle = "Placed at random within each district"
)
```

## Bubble map

We show each district as one dot. Dot size shows the population in 2031. Dot color
shows density. A large, dark dot shows many people in a small area.

```{r bubble-map, fig.alt = "Map of India with one dot per district, sized by population and colored by density."}
plot_bubble_map(districts, "total_millions", "density_2031",
  title = "Population and density by district, 2031",
  size_breaks = c(1, 5, 10, 15), size_title = "People, millions",
  trans = "log10", limits = c(10, 50000), oob = scales::squish,
  breaks = c(10, 100, 1000, 10000), labels = scales::label_comma(),
  color_title = "People per km²"
)
```

## One dot per 100,000 people

Here, each dot shows 100,000 people. The dots are close together where density is
high. We put each dot at a random position in its district. One dot does not show
a real location.

```{r dot-density, fig.alt = "Map of India with one dot per 100,000 people."}
set.seed(2031)
plot_dot_density_map(districts, "total_2031",
  title = "One dot for every 100,000 people, 2031",
  subtitle = "Placed at random within each district"
)
```

## Change in density

Next, we map the change in density from 2011 to 2031. District area is constant.
This change is equal to the change in population.

Density falls in some districts, for example New Delhi, Mumbai, and Ratnagiri. In
these districts, the IIPS tables give a smaller share of the state population.

The scale stops at 60%. Daman and Dadra & Nagar Haveli are above this limit. MoHFW
projects small union territories from their growth rates for 1981 to 2011. Do not
use these two values.

```{r change-map, fig.alt = "District map of India of the change in density from 2011 to 2031."}
plot_map(districts, "density_change",
  title = "Change in density by district, 2011 to 2031",
  palette = "blue_red", midpoint = 0, limits = c(-60, 60), oob = scales::squish,
  breaks = c(-60, -30, 0, 30, 60),
  labels = c("-60% or less", "-30%", "0", "+30%", "+60% or more"),
  legend_title = "Change in density", na_color = "grey85",
  show_state_boundaries = TRUE, state_boundary_color = "grey30", state_boundary_width = 0.2
)
```

## Rural density and urban population

Next, we show two measures on one map. The fill shows rural density. The dots show
urban population. This package calculates these figures. Use this map only to
compare areas.

```{r rural-urban, fig.alt = "District map of India of rural density, with dots for urban population."}
plot_map(districts, "rural_density_2031",
  title = "Rural density and urban population by district, 2031",
  palette = "greens", trans = "log10", limits = c(1, 3000), oob = scales::squish,
  breaks = c(1, 10, 100, 1000), labels = scales::label_comma(),
  legend_title = "Rural people per km²", na_color = "grey85",
  show_state_boundaries = TRUE, state_boundary_color = "white", state_boundary_width = 0.2
) +
  census_bubble_layer(
    filter(districts, urban_2031 > 0), "urban_millions",
    max_size = 6, size_breaks = c(1, 5, 10, 15), size_title = "Urban people, millions"
  )
```

## Below the district level

District totals hide the local pattern. `get_census_boundaries(2011, "village", state = ...)`
gives village and town polygons for one state, and `attach_geometry()` joins them
to the census by code. We use the 2011 Census population, because projections do
not go to individual towns.

We use Haryana, because polygons cover all of its population. Coverage is not
the same in all states. The polygons do not include most large city corporations,
so they cover 74.5% of the population of India. Do a check of the coverage before
you use a different state. Do not use the Delhi file. Its populations do not agree
with the census.

```{r haryana-data}
haryana <- bind_rows(
  at_level(census_2011_demographics(), "village", sector = "rural"),
  at_level(census_2011_demographics(), "town", sector = "urban")
) |>
  filter(state_name_harmonized == "Haryana") |>
  distinct(town_village_code, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  attach_geometry(2011, geography = "village", unmatched = "ignore") |>
  filter(!st_is_empty(geometry))

by_level <- list(
  District = haryana |>
    group_by(district_code) |>
    summarise(population = sum(population)),
  Subdistrict = haryana |>
    group_by(district_code, subdistrict_code) |>
    summarise(population = sum(population), .groups = "drop"),
  `Village and town` = haryana
) |>
  lapply(function(d) mutate(d, density = population / area_km2(d)))

tibble::tibble(
  Level = names(by_level),
  Units = vapply(by_level, nrow, integer(1)),
  `Median density` = round(vapply(by_level, function(d) median(d$density), numeric(1))),
  `Highest density` = round(vapply(by_level, function(d) max(d$density), numeric(1)))
) |>
  knitr::kable(format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

The maps use one scale. Each map has the same people and the same area. Only the
size of the units changes. Gray areas on the village map are the 199 villages
with no population.

```{r haryana-maps, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "Density maps of Haryana at district, subdistrict and village level."}
compare_maps(
  by_level, "density",
  palette = "oranges", limits = c(30, 30000), trans = "log10", oob = scales::squish,
  breaks = c(100, 1000, 10000), labels = scales::label_comma(),
  legend_title = "People per km²", show_state_boundaries = FALSE, base_layer = FALSE,
  legend_position = "bottom"
) &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The village and town polygons come from the
[National Water Data Portal](https://nwdp.nwic.gov.in/dataset/9bad17f2-9d88-428d-98ad-831ef01ae2e4).
We calculate the area of each unit from its polygon, so these values are not the
same as the published census density.
